evidence: ProjectController.ts, TaskController.ts and UserController.ts each declare a class with constructor-injected use cases and a `routes(): Router` method, so all three follow the same controller pattern.
All three import `readBody` and `requiredString` from '../RequestParsing'. ProjectController.ts also imports `optionalString` and `BadRequestError`, so body parsing is handled in one shared place.
ProjectController.ts defines `queryString(req, field)`, which appears only in this file and throws the shared `BadRequestError`. Nothing is duplicated across files.
ProjectController.addTask and listTasks are served on '/projects/:projectId/tasks', a nested resource route. TaskController handles '/tasks/:taskId/...' actions, so the two controllers don't overlap.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All three files do one job: adapting HTTP requests to application use cases. Each controller follows the same shape. It takes its use cases through the constructor, exposes `routes(): Router`, parses input with the shared helpers in `../RequestParsing` (`readBody`, `requiredString`, `optionalString`, `BadRequestError`), and turns use-case results into JSON responses. No file skips those helpers or repeats a validation rule. ProjectController has a small private `queryString` helper that exists only in that file. It reuses the shared `BadRequestError`, so nothing is duplicated. It could arguably move to RequestParsing, but as written it doesn't break the rule. ProjectController also handles task creation and listing, but under the nested route `/projects/:projectId/tasks`, which is a normal way to organise REST resources. It isn't a separate concern.
